goals: Diagnose them from training vs test error
why: Every modelling decision (depth, number of features, regularisation, more data) is a move along the bias–variance trade-off. It is the most useful mental model in ML.
explain: **Bias** is error from being too simple: a straight line through a curved relationship. The model is wrong in the same way on training and test data. That is **underfitting**.

**Variance** is error from being too sensitive to the specific training sample: a wiggly curve through every point. It scores brilliantly on training data and poorly on new data. That is **overfitting**.
A tailor analogy: a one-size-fits-all T-shirt (high bias) fits nobody well; a suit tailored to one exact pose (high variance) fits only that pose. You want a good fit that still allows movement.

Diagnose: **high train error + high test error** = bias. **Low train error + much higher test error** = variance. Remedies for bias: more features, a more flexible model. Remedies for variance: more data, regularisation, a simpler model, ensembles.

formula.plain: Total error = being systematically wrong + being unstable + randomness you can never remove.

example.title: Three trees on the same loan data
steps: Depth 1: train 70%, test 69% → both low = high bias
Depth 15: train 100%, test 72% → big gap = high variance
example.result: Depth 4 wins. The "sweet spot" is where test error is lowest, not where training error is lowest.

mistakes: Adding complexity to fix a variance problem (it makes it worse).
Assuming more data always helps: it reduces variance, not bias.
takeaways: Underfit = too simple; overfit = memorised noise
Compare train vs test error to diagnose

practice.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X, y = make_moons(600, noise=0.35, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
for d in [1, 3, 5, 10, None]:
    m = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(d, round(m.score(X_tr, y_tr), 3), round(m.score(X_te, y_te), 3))

check.q: Train error 2%, test error 25%. The problem is…
check.why: A large train–test gap signals overfitting.

options: A more flexible model or better features
check.why: Bias means the model is too simple.
